description: Merhabalar biz DİYARBAKIR FİNAL OKULLARI 7/F den Erva Duru Söylemez, Elif Balık, Elif Su Dere NASA SPACE APPS yarışmasına katılma amacımız astronotun uzaydaki güvenliğini korumak. Yaptığımız proje astronotun uzay yürüyüşü yaptığında veya ISS'nin dışına çıkması durumunda astronota gelebilecek uzay çöpleri veya enkaz parçalarının astronota gelmesini hazırladığımız sistem aracılığıyla engellemek. İyi günler dileriz
summary:
ASTROKOR, developed by the Galaxy X team (Erva Duru Söylemez, Elif Su Dere, and Elif Balık) for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, is a wearable space debris early-warning and decision-support system designed to maximize astronaut safety during Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) against hypervelocity debris threats and the Kessler Syndrome.

The system features a hybrid detection architecture that combines long-range ISS and ground-based radar systems with short-range LiDAR and infrared sensors to monitor a 50-meter safety zone and a critical intervention range of 5–10 meters.

Using Kalman filters for precise motion prediction and orbital analysis, ASTROKOR delivers instant, multi-channel alerts through helmet-mounted Head-Up Displays (HUDs) and 360-degree haptic shoulder vibration motors that indicate the exact direction of approaching threats.

Additionally, the project includes an interactive Three.js WebGL 3D simulator featuring MMU jetpack controls (W-A-S-D), real-time telemetry, and secure offline execution to ensure seamless jury presentations.
details:
1. Introduction and Problem Definition: The Invisible Threat in Low Earth Orbit

Humanity’s activities in space exploration and satellite technologies have been growing exponentially in recent years, transforming Low Earth Orbit (LEO) into an increasingly crowded traffic environment. With the deployment of communication networks, Earth observation satellites, scientific research platforms, and commercial space stations, millions of debris fragments generated by defunct satellites, spent rocket stages, and orbital collisions now pose a serious threat to space operations.

According to official debris catalogs maintained by international space agencies and NASA, Low Earth Orbit contains more than 36,000 trackable objects larger than 10 centimeters, approximately 1 million high-energy fragments between 1 and 10 centimeters that are difficult to monitor with radar systems, and over 100 million micro-debris particles ranging from 1 millimeter to 1 centimeter.

These objects travel at an average orbital velocity of 7.8 kilometers per second (approximately 28,000 km/h). At such extreme relative speeds, even a tiny paint flake or metal fragment only a few millimeters in diameter can behave like a projectile and easily penetrate the hull of a spacecraft or the pressurized suit of an astronaut performing an Extravehicular Activity (EVA). Throughout spaceflight history, more than 660 orbital explosion and collision events have occurred, making the risk of the Kessler Syndrome, a cascade of uncontrollable collisions in orbit, increasingly realistic.

Current debris-monitoring operations rely primarily on ground-based radar stations and the centralized telemetry systems of the International Space Station (ISS). However, these macro-scale systems generally focus on protecting the station as a whole and are often incapable of providing millisecond-level warnings to astronauts regarding sudden local threats at the centimeter or millimeter scale. It is physically impossible for human vision and muscle reflexes alone to react to an object approaching at 7.8 km/s.

ASTROKOR has been developed precisely to fill this critical gap by providing astronauts with a personal, autonomous, and proactive protective shield while operating in the harsh environment of space.

2. Operating Principle and Hybrid Detection Architecture

ASTROKOR is built upon a multi-layered hybrid sensing architecture that does not rely solely on a single sensor technology or ground-based data sources. The system combines macro-scale space traffic information with micro-scale local sensor measurements in real time to create a dynamic safety shield around the astronaut.

The detection and processing workflow consists of three primary stages:

1. Long-Range Macro Data Integration

At the first layer, the system utilizes International Space Station telemetry streams, catalog data provided by NASA and global space surveillance networks, and ground-based radar predictions. This enables continuous monitoring of orbital traffic density and known large-object trajectories within the astronaut's operational corridor.

2. Close-Range Local Scanning (50 m and 5-10 m Volumes)

The ASTROKOR module continuously scans the astronaut’s entire 360-degree surroundings, including blind spots beyond the astronaut’s field of view, using high-precision LiDAR and infrared (IR) sensor arrays.

This monitoring process is managed through two critical safety zones:

50-Meter Early Warning Zone

The outer security perimeter where an approaching object first enters the local sensor network. At this stage, the system enters a caution state and begins trajectory analysis.

5-10 Meter Critical Intervention Zone

The final line of defense, where collision probability exceeds a critical threshold and the astronaut must immediately perform an avoidance maneuver using MMU (Manned Maneuvering Unit) thrusters or tether-assisted movement.

3. Kalman Filter and Trajectory Prediction Algorithm

Sensor measurements in space can contain noise due to solar flares, cosmic radiation, and sudden changes in lighting conditions. The ASTROKOR software core incorporates a Kalman Filter algorithm that removes measurement uncertainty from raw sensor data and calculates the object's position, velocity vector, and TCA (Time to Closest Approach) within milliseconds.

As a result, harmless objects that will safely pass by the astronaut are filtered out, while only genuine collision threats are escalated for action.

3. Multi-Channel Decision Support and Human-Machine Interface (HMI)

In emergency situations, asking astronauts to interpret complex numerical information or listen to lengthy audio instructions can waste valuable seconds. Therefore, ASTROKOR delivers warnings simultaneously through two sensory channels designed according to human physiological and cognitive ergonomics principles.

Helmet-Mounted Head-Up Display (HUD)

A minimalist, high-contrast visual interface projected onto the astronaut’s visor displays:

  • Distance to the nearest threat (meters)
  • Estimated Time to Closest Approach (TCA)
  • Relative velocity
  • Recommended avoidance direction

Commands such as “Move Left” or “Descend” are presented using clear directional arrows. To prevent visual fatigue, the display remains inactive during normal operations and activates only when a safety zone is breached.

360-Degree Haptic Shoulder Feedback System

One of the most innovative components of the project is its haptic warning mechanism. High-precision vibration motors are placed on the astronaut’s right shoulder, left shoulder, and back.

The direction from which debris approaches determines which motors activate and at what frequency. This allows threat information to be transmitted directly to the astronaut’s nervous system and reflex pathways.

For example, if debris approaches from the rear-right direction, the right shoulder and back motors vibrate, intuitively prompting the astronaut to maneuver forward-left without needing to turn their head or check the display.

4. Benefits and Intended Impact

Integrating ASTROKOR into space operations offers significant advantages for both immediate mission safety and the long-term sustainability of the space economy.

Maximum Astronaut Safety

Reduces the risks of suit penetration, oxygen leakage, depressurization, and potentially fatal injuries caused by debris impacts during EVAs.

Reduced Cognitive Workload

Allows astronauts to focus on complex repair, maintenance, and assembly tasks without constantly monitoring their surroundings for hazards.

Mission Continuity and Cost Efficiency

Decreases the likelihood of EVA interruptions caused by unexpected debris threats, contributing to the uninterrupted execution of space operations worth billions of dollars.

Standardization for Future Space Missions

Establishes a scalable wearable safety standard for future Artemis lunar missions, commercial space stations, and emerging space tourism activities.

5. Engineering Considerations Incorporated During Development

The Galaxy X team designed ASTROKOR not merely as a theoretical concept but as a solution grounded in real-world aerospace engineering constraints and operational realities.

1. Non-Invasive Spacesuit Integration

Current NASA and SpaceX EVA suits undergo strict certification and safety testing. Modifying suit fabrics or routing cables through pressure layers could jeopardize suit integrity.

Therefore, ASTROKOR is designed as a completely external and modular attachment that can be mounted and removed without any structural modifications to existing spacesuits.

2. False Positive Reduction

A system that continuously generates alarms in a dense debris environment could lead to desensitization, distraction, and panic.

ASTROKOR mitigates this issue through Kalman filter-based vector analysis that identifies and prioritizes only objects with genuine collision potential.

3. Thermal Management and Radiation Resistance

Astronauts operating in Low Earth Orbit experience temperature fluctuations ranging from approximately +120°C in direct sunlight to −150°C in Earth’s shadow.

To address these harsh conditions, system components are protected by Multi-Layer Insulation (MLI) and utilize radiation-resistant, low-power microprocessors.

4. Optical Blind Spot and Solar Glare Protection

Direct solar exposure may temporarily blind optical or LiDAR sensors. To maintain uninterrupted operation, ASTROKOR employs redundant sensing through infrared thermal monitoring and radar telemetry data.

6. Software Infrastructure, Simulation Environment, and Innovation Approach

To validate technical accuracy and evaluate operational scenarios, our team developed an interactive 3D Space Debris Simulator using Three.js and WebGL technologies.

Built with modern software development tools and algorithmic modeling techniques, this simulation environment enables astronauts to maneuver through three-dimensional space using MMU jetpack controls (W-A-S-D and Q-E keys), while experiencing:

  • Single-debris encounter scenarios
  • Multi-object Kessler Syndrome debris storms
  • Critical 10-meter intervention tests
  • Real-time telemetry-based threat simulations

Furthermore, the simulator has been designed to operate offline through local devices using file:/// access, eliminating dependence on external servers and ensuring maximum data security and uninterrupted accessibility during presentations, testing sessions, and mission planning.

The most distinctive and innovative aspect of ASTROKOR is its inversion of the traditional centralized-control philosophy in space safety. Rather than requiring astronauts to interpret complex radar information, the system translates danger into an immediate and intuitive tactile reflex.

By allowing astronauts to literally feel approaching threats through haptic feedback on their shoulders, ASTROKOR introduces a new paradigm in EVA safety and opens the door to the next generation of human-centered space protection systems.

Micro-Debris Between 1 mm and 1 cm: More than 100 million millimeter-sized particles capable of penetrating spacesuit layers. Conjunction Assessment (Collision Avoidance) Data: Warning matrices updated daily by NASA and space surveillance networks, calculating when objects will make their closest approach to spacecraft or astronauts (TCA – Time of Closest Approach).
